summary.text: River-god of Thessaly, born to Oceanus and Tethys among the eddying streams of the world — father of the nymph Daphne, whom Apollo pursued until she became the laurel, and of Cyrene, whom the god carried off from his marsh-meadow to Libya.

story.text: Hesiod names Peneus in the first family of waters: when Tethys lay with Oceanus she bore the eddying rivers, and among them holy Simois and Peneus, set in one breath with Alpheus, Strymon, and Achelous — the Thessalian stream counted among the great brotherhood of Potamoi.

Ovid sets Apollo's first love on his banks. Daphne, daughter of Peneus, prayed her father that she might live unwed like Diana; when Cupid's leaden shaft made her flee the sun-god's pursuit through Tempe, she looked to her father's waves and prayed that her beauty be destroyed — and before the prayer ended bark closed her breast and the laurel stood where the maiden had been.

Apollonius tells a second Thessalian tale on the same river. Cyrene once tended sheep along the marsh-meadow of Peneus in Haemonia, holding maidenhood dear; as she guarded her flock by the stream, Apollo carried her off far from Thessaly to Libya, where she bore him Aristaeus. Hyginus names her explicitly: 'Aristaeus by Cyrene, daughter of Peneus.'

Heracles too knew the Thessalian water. When he cleansed the stables of Augeas, Apollodorus says, he diverted the courses of the Alpheus and Peneus through the cattle-yard — twin rivers turned to one labour in the Peloponnese and Thessaly alike.
